newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Foreign investors desert Bulgaria treasury market.
newsitem.headline: Foreign investors desert Bulgaria treasury market.

text.p: Rapidly declining interest rates on Bulgarian treasury bills, reflecting excessive lev liquidity and high demand, have discouraged foreign investment in local securities, bankers said on Friday.

"More than 60 percent of around $250 million invested in local treasuries has pulled out to other regions like Russia and Ukraine, where earnings are higher," Albert Trayner, treasurer of Raiffeisenbank Bulgaria AD, told Reuters.

High yields at the beginning of the year and expectations of low exchange rate risk under a currency board system introduced on July 1 attracted some $300 million in foreign investment in government paper in the past few months, the Finance Ministry said.

Interest rates have come down to 0.58 percent monthly from 18 percent in March, reflecting stabilisation of the economy following an International Monetary Fund reform and funding deal reached in March.
The central bank cut the annual rate to 6.96 percent from July 14.

"I am not concerned by the outflow of foreign investors in our treasuries. We have raised so far sufficient funds for the budget from domestic investors," Plamen Oresharski, head of the Finance Ministry Treasury and Debt Department, told Reuters.

"I do not expect any dramatic events as far as interest rates are concerned until the year-end. I expect rates to bounce back to 10 to 12 percent annually," said Oresharski, also a deputy finance minister.
Bulgaria's currency board system anchoring the lev to the mark bans central bank lending to the government and commercial banks.
With a fixed exchange rate regime and a stagnant stock market, where floor trading is suspended, banks are left with few investment alternatives.
"If the central bank, through management of the debt, gets the rates back in the range of 14 to 18 percent on an annualised basis, then it could attract foreign investors," said Trayner.
"If foreigners looking at Bulgaria are nervous about possibilities of the currency board not working, they probably will not come into Bulgaria unless they can earn 20 percent."
Other analysts were optimistic on Bulgaria sustaining the currency board as long as the government pursued reform.

"The economic outlook in the coming months is going to look better. In the coming six months to a year we are going to see stronger growth, lower inflation and a better budget position," said Deutsche Morgan Grenfell Emerging Market Analyst Stuart Parkinson.

A three to five percent T-bill yield pickup will not be high enough for foreign investors to come back but once the equity market has revived, it is likely to attract more foreign investment, he added.
Bulgaria is expected to re-open its stock exchange by the year-end.
It entered the currency board with a good foreign exchange reserve position and official lending will protect the currency board in the coming months, said Parkinson.
"There is a very low chance that the currency board will fail in the first year of its life. The next years will depend on how good reforms are," he added. -- Sofia Newsroom, 359-2-981-4145
